item.title: AI arms race giving way to AI returns race: Aditya Birla Group chairman
item.description: Aditya Birla Group chairman Kumar Mangalam Birla says businesses are taking a measured approach to AI investments, focusing on tangible returns, productivity and capital allocation ...
item.dc:creator: Our Bureau
item.content:encoded: Aditya Birla Group chairman Kumar Mangalam Birla said investments in artificial intelligence (AI) were becoming more calibrated as businesses assessed the tangible returns from such investments, adding that a shift from an AI arms race to an AI returns race was underway. “If I think about a year ago, we probably thought that AI was a monster sitting there on the last row, and it would eat me up by the time I got here if I didn't know everything about AI, and so there was a sense of trepidation and fear. That now doesn't exist. The shift is from an AI arms race, which is getting the right compute, right talent to an AI returns race, in the sense, what does this AI do for me? What is the return I get from investing in AI? Where does that stack up in my capital allocated pyramid?” Speaking at a panel discussion at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in Delhi, Birla noted that apprehensions about what AI could do had ebbed and discussions were now more centred on what it could deliver for businesses, including those within the Aditya Birla Group, while noting that investments in AI could not be made simply based on the fear of missing out. “We're going to take it a little more gradually than we thought a year ago because it is a large investment, and I don't think we need to act out of a sense of FOMO… I think we're being thoughtful about it, and like I said, asking ourselves what's the return on the investment you can make,” he said. He added that the group was unravelling the impact of AI on productivity across the entire organisation, but there were specific applications that were yielding results, for instance, in customer interface, manufacturing efficiencies and increasing net interest margins in the group’s financial business. Birla added that capital allocation for the large and diversified group, shifting geopolitics and keeping people enthused were important elements for the growth of the business. “You can't stop growing. So for me, capital allocation has been a challenge because you have a whole lot of new demands on your capital, which we know about. You either grow or you go down. You can't stay in a state of equilibrium. The other one clearly has been geopolitics, because we are a global organization. When I read about a significant global event in the newspapers, I can be sure that it will impact us somewhere,” he said. The Aditya Birla Group, headed by Kumar Mangalam Birla, operates across more than 20 sectors in 41 countries spanning six continents, employs over 2.27 lakh people and has more than 600 manufacturing units. It reported revenue of around $72 billion in FY26 and earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) of $8.5 billion. He added that the lines between important and urgent were blurring, as keeping morale high in a people-run organisation was crucial. “Getting them to keep their chin up, getting them to collaborate and learn from each other, learn from outside… at the end of the day, it's people who make the difference, and I think keeping them going and keeping them enthused and energetic is an equally important task,” he said. On ensuring businesses stay strong, Birla said continuous training and stable operations were critical for achieving scale at low costs. He noted that the group's manufacturing businesses aim to be in the bottom decile of the global cost curve, that is, among the 10 per cent lowest-cost producers. The group's cement capacity touched 200 million tonnes this year, making it the largest cement company in the world outside China, and it has added 2 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity to the cement business. “Moving knowledge around from one business to the other, moving people around from one business to the other, which we do in a very systematic way, I think all of these help to sort of keep the businesses up to speed, and I think global best practices we've actually in some of our businesses set the global benchmark,” he said.

item.title: Rupee should be allowed to find its own level, says Uday Kotak
item.description: Uday Kotak says the rupee should find its own level, urging India to boost competitiveness, innovation and manufacturing while keeping investment options open ...
item.dc:creator: Shubham Kumar
item.content:encoded: Uday Kotak, founder and non-executive director of Kotak Mahindra Bank, on Tuesday said the rupee should be allowed to find its own footing. “My personal view is we should let the rupee find its own level. And over time, the true strength of the economy will play out,” Kotak said in a panel discussion at Bloomberg New Economy Forum.   After depreciating close to 7% in the last one year, the rupee gained 1.5 per cent in the last two trading sessions after steps by the Reserve Bank of India, aimed at curbing speculative bets. Kotak said a concentration in seven to ten stocks globally is attracting the most portfolio flows, and that this might be reassessed by investors. “India has to consider this as an important signal that we need to do a lot more to be competitive, efficient, self-reliant, and stronger in our research and innovation.” Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have pulled a record Rs 3.08 trillion out of Indian equities in just nine months of calendar year 2026 – nearly double the Rs1.66 trillion withdrawn in 2025. The outflow has exerted pressure on the rupee, which has depreciated 5.7 per cent in 2026 so far. The central bank has also intervened in the foreign exchange market to curb undue volatility. Kotak said Indian companies should enhance their partnerships with Chinese firms while Western capital turns more transactional. “If there are joint ventures between Chinese and Indian companies for manufacturing in India – the game China played with the US many years ago – that could be a path forward for India.”  Historically, Kotak said, India has tended to look to the West for investment. “But with the challenges, particularly from the United States and overall a more transactional approach to investment, the time has come for India to keep all its options open.”  Speaking at the same panel discussion, Surendra Rosha, Co-CEO, Asia & Middle East, HSBC, said that while negotiating the US-China divide in the technological stack may be harder to manage for India, the comforting reality is that the country has a history of managing different poles of power. Waleed Al Mokarrab Al Muhairi, Deputy Group chief executive officer, Mubadala Investment Company, said a fragmented world is here to stay. “We don't view it as a kind of short-term blip. It is the new normal, at least for the next five, ten, maybe even 15 years,” he said, adding that India’s favourable demographics, ability to adopt technology quickly and a massive infrastructure push, coupled with deep markets undergoing reforms, are enablers for the country. (Disclosure: Entities controlled by the Kotak family have a significant holding in Business Standard Pvt. Ltd)

item.title: Nilekani panel explores last-minute question papers to prevent exam leaks
item.description: The task force is considering large question banks, AI-generated papers and wider computer-based testing to prevent leaks, with recommendations expected within three months of its formation ...
item.dc:creator: Auhona Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: The Centre’s task force on examination reforms is considering generating question papers at the last minute from a large question bank to prevent leaks. The panel is expected to submit its recommendations within three months of its formation on July 28, Nandan Nilekani, who heads the high-powered task force, said on Tuesday. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, Nilekani said the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (Undergraduate), or Neet (UG), paper leak had raised questions about the need for conventional question papers, given the financial incentive to obtain and sell them in advance. “So I think the question becomes, why do we need to have something called a question paper? Because the moment you have a question paper, that creates an economic incentive for that to be sold. So the way to do it is to really have a massive bank of questions. And only at the last minute, generate the question paper for that day,” he said. This approach would remove the financial incentive to obtain and sell question papers in advance, he added. Nilekani said artificial intelligence (AI) could also be used to generate question papers on the day of an examination to prevent leaks. The panel is also examining the expansion of computer-based testing, which would require a wider network of examination centres, he said. India currently has around 150,000 locations where candidates can take tests, and this network needs to expand, Nilekani observed. “We have 150,000 locations where a young boy or girl can take a test. That needs to be expanded. So I think these are all systemic issues which we will address in our committee,” he said. The committee would identify the root causes of examination-related problems and use technology to address systemic weaknesses, Nilekani said, adding that Prime Minister Narendra Modi was keen to implement its recommendations. Modi announced the formation of a high-powered task force led by the Infosys cofounder on July 26, following protests over the Neet (UG) 2026 paper leak and demands for accountability in the examination system. The Centre subsequently informed the Supreme Court that the panel would recommend reforms to strengthen the security and credibility of competitive examinations, particularly those conducted by the National Testing Agency. AI could help India improve literacy and numeracy among millions of people, Nilekani said. AI tools could also make information more accessible by allowing people to interact with computers in their preferred languages, he added. Nilekani dismissed concerns that AI would lead to widespread job losses in India’s information technology services sector, calling the argument “absolutely hogwash”. Companies would need greater support to fundamentally transform their operations using AI, creating more work for technology services firms, he said. “I think this is all disaster marketing to suit the interests of large capital. The fact of the matter is that the requirement for companies like Infosys or others is actually more than ever before because the transformation of enterprise is a very complex activity. And AI requires fundamentally reimagining the way you do business. And it’s a root and branch surgery that is required. And this, in fact, even more requires firms like ours to show companies how to go about making those transformations, how to reimagine the future,” he said. Nilekani said companies would need to transform their operations, reskill workers, and build new capabilities to adopt AI, adding that the technology’s capabilities were far ahead of its deployment. While AI coding agents would make coding more productive, he said, most of the work in technology projects extended beyond coding to include governance, change management, and business transformation. New jobs would emerge in understanding client requirements, coordinating teams, and ensuring AI systems did not hallucinate or behave unpredictably, he added. Small businesses could become a major source of job creation if AI improved their productivity and gave them better access to markets, capital, and information, Nilekani said. Millions of small enterprises could expand and hire more workers as a result, he added. India’s strength lay in applying AI at scale rather than competing solely to build models and computing infrastructure, Nilekani said, citing the country’s experience with digital public infrastructure such as Aadhaar and the Unified Payments Interface.

item.title: Data centre demand to outstrip supply as AI usage grows, say experts
item.description: NTT Data and Brookfield executives expect strong data centre demand amid rising AI adoption, but warn that power infrastructure, skilled talent and capacity constraints pose challenges ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Technology / Tech News / Data centre demand to outstrip supply as AI usage grows, say experts

Data centre demand to outstrip supply as AI usage grows, say experts NTT Data and Brookfield executives expect strong data centre demand amid rising AI adoption, but warn that power infrastructure, skilled talent and capacity constraints pose challenges

Data centre infrastructure is expanding to meet rising demand for AI computing capacity

Aashish Aryan New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 9:04 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Electricity grid capacity, energy storage and conversion, and the talent needed to run data centres remain the biggest bottlenecks to expanding data centres globally and in India, Abhijit Dubey, president and chief executive officer (CEO) of NTT Data, said on Tuesday.   “The biggest bottleneck nobody talks about is the hidden bottleneck of talent. So, if you think about electricians, skilled technicians, design, construction... their compensation today is more than most of the white-collar jobs,” Dubey said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 here.   There was, however, no dearth of demand for new data centres or even the capital to invest in the sector, he said.

The narrative of the demand for artificial intelligence (AI), the compute, capacity, the energy and supply chain for AI being fragile is misplaced, and not connected to ground realities, said Connor Teskey, the CEO of Brookfield Asset Management.   “We hear about a more efficient model, and people worry about the demand picture, or we hear about one data centre being released and people worry about the demand picture. The demand so overwhelms supply at this point that there is going to be a supply-demand imbalance through the end of this decade and probably far beyond that,” Teskey said. Also Read

Beyond Nvidia: Why tech firms are turning to custom chips for AI inference

Dubey and Teskey were part of a panel discussion that also included Infosys CEO and Managing Director (MD) Salil Parekh and Sajiv Ahuja, chairman and CEO of Tillman Global Holdings.

Responding to a question on the data centre capacity buildout, Parekh, however, said that as semiconductor chips were "massively expensive" and facing tremendous competition, it was unclear how long the data centre capacity being built would remain useful.   “Today the demand is fantastic, but these are some of the risks that could play out," Parekh said.   A second risk, he said, was the backlash against such massive build-out, and that the social response, especially in Western markets, needed to be balanced with the geography’s economic drivers.   AI services are growing at a double-digit rate sequentially and are likely to drive almost half of Infosys' work in two to three years, Parekh said.

"It is growing at a fantastic pace. If you extrapolate that by a few quarters, you already start to see that's 20-30 per cent of our work in a few quarters, and maybe in two or three years, almost half of our work," he said.   More From This Section
